title: Romans 4:13–25
context: Paul presses the Abraham argument further. The promise that Abraham would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all his offspring. Abraham believed God who gives life to the dead, trusting the promise against all natural hope, and his faith was counted as righteousness. Paul says this was written for believers today as well. Both traditions read the passage as a celebration of faith resting on God’s promise. They differ on how faith arises and on what makes the promise “sure.”

verses.text: For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he would be heir of the world wasn’t through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
verses.arminianNotes: The promise came through the righteousness of faith, not through the law. Both traditions see the promise resting on faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise grounded in God’s covenant grace.

verses.text: For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void, and the promise is made of no effect.
verses.arminianNotes: If heirs come through the law, faith is empty and the promise void. Both traditions see law and promise as different principles.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that any reliance on law would cancel grace.

verses.text: For the law produces wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there disobedience.
verses.arminianNotes: The law brings wrath; where there is no law there is no transgression. Both traditions see the law exposing sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the law’s condemning function.

verses.text: For this cause it is of faith, that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise may be sure to all the offspring, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all.
verses.arminianNotes:
It depends on faith so that it may rest on grace and the promise be guaranteed to all the offspring. Arminian readers see faith as the condition that keeps salvation gracious, since faith receives rather than earns. The promise is sure to everyone who believes.

Arminian readers also note that the guarantee belongs to those who continue in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the guarantee resting on God’s grace rather than human performance. Because God gives the faith he requires, the promise cannot fail for any of his people.
verses.keyContrast: Both agree that faith keeps the promise a matter of grace. Arminian readers see the promise guaranteed to all who believe and continue in faith. Reformed readers see it guaranteed because God himself secures the faith of the elect.

verses.text: As it is written, “I have made you a father of many nations.” This is in the presence of him whom he believed: God, who gives life to the dead, and calls the things that are not, as though they were.
verses.arminianNotes: Abraham believed God, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence what does not exist. Both traditions see faith resting on God’s creative power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a parallel with regeneration, in which God gives life where there was none.

verses.text: Against hope, Abraham in hope believed, to the end that he might become a father of many nations, according to that which had been spoken, “So will your offspring be.”
verses.arminianNotes: In hope against hope Abraham believed. Both traditions see faith trusting the promise despite circumstances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faith as confidence in God’s word.

verses.text: Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb.
verses.arminianNotes: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his body and Sarah’s barrenness. Both traditions see faith facing reality honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faith that looks past natural impossibility.

verses.text: Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God,
verses.arminianNotes: No unbelief made him waver; he grew strong in faith, giving glory to God. Arminian readers see faith as Abraham’s real response, strengthened as he trusted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God strengthening Abraham’s faith, so that the glory goes to God.

verses.text: and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.
verses.arminianNotes: He was fully convinced that God was able to do what he promised. Both traditions agree that faith rests on God’s ability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see assurance grounded in God’s power.

verses.text: Therefore it also was “credited to him for righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes: That is why his faith was counted to him as righteousness. See the note on verse 3. Both traditions agree that faith, not works, is the means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faith receiving imputed righteousness.

verses.text: Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone,
verses.arminianNotes: The words were not written for Abraham alone. Both traditions see Scripture applying to all believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see one way of salvation in both testaments.

verses.text: but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,
verses.arminianNotes: They were written for us also, who believe in him who raised Jesus. Arminian readers see the same offer extended to all who believe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise applied to believers today.

verses.text: who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. Both traditions see the cross and resurrection as the ground of justification.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s resurrection as God’s vindication of his finished work.
